title: US Proposes Tariffs of Up to 25% on India; GTRI Urges New Delhi to Reject Deal
excerpt: Washington's Section 301 excess-capacity findings offer India 17% if it signs a trade agreement — a dual rate the GTRI think tank calls coercive bait.
body:
• The United States has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods under a Section 301 investigation into "structural excess capacity," with a lower 17% rate if India signs a reciprocal trade agreement.
  • The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) calls the dual rate a "calculated bait" to extract one-sided concessions and urges India to reject a deal signed under that pressure.
  • India's Commerce Ministry says it is examining the notice and maintains that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.
  • For Indian exporters and US importers: the duties are proposed, not in force — public comments run until January 5, 2027, with hearings scheduled for January 25.

The United States has proposed tariffs of up to 25 percent on Indian goods, alleging that India's manufacturing policies contribute to "structural excess capacity" and distort global trade, according to the US Trade Representative's notice reported by Forbes India. Washington has also proposed considering a lower rate of 17 percent if India reaches a reciprocal trade agreement that addresses the investigation's findings.

The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), a New Delhi trade think tank, responded by urging India to reject a deal struck on those terms. In its report, covered by The Hindu BusinessLine, GTRI said the proposed tariffs "recreate the reciprocal-tariff regime under a new name," with lower rates for countries that sign agreements and higher baseline duties for those that refuse.

"The offering of India a 17% deal rate (versus 25% without a pact) is a calculated bait designed to show a marginal 1%-3% tariff edge over rivals like Bangladesh, Vietnam, and China."

— Global Trade Research Initiative report

What the investigation examined

The investigations were launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, covering 16 economies. The USTR has now issued determinations for 14 of them, including India, China, Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Bangladesh, the European Union, and Taiwan; Mexico and Norway were not included in the latest determinations. India faces the second-highest proposed rate, behind Vietnam at 35 percent, while the proposed agreement rates for China and Vietnam are 20 percent and Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia and Thailand face 18 percent.

In India, the USTR examined industrial policies aimed at expanding manufacturing, labour protections, financial policies, market-access barriers and imports and investment from non-market economies, particularly China. The investigation flagged potential excess capacity or export surpluses in seven Indian sectors, GTRI noted: solar modules, petrochemicals, steel, textiles, health-related goods, construction materials and automotive products. GTRI's Ajay Srivastava has also said Washington is questioning India's Production Linked Incentive and Make in India schemes while shielding its own manufacturers with tariffs.

India's response, and GTRI's counter-argument

India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said it had taken note of the notice and that it was under examination, reiterating that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector and that trade concerns should be addressed through the ongoing negotiations for an India-US Bilateral Trade Agreement.

GTRI argued that capacity should be assessed against domestic consumption, export markets and future demand — not exports alone — noting that India's solar module capacity is nearly three times domestic demand. It also pointed out that the proposed tariff relief does not require countries to change their industrial capacity at all, which it said undermines the investigation's stated rationale. The think tank warned that the threat of so-called Graham tariffs of up to 100 percent continues to hang over India, and recommended that New Delhi answer the allegations sector by sector.

What happens next

The proposed tariffs are not yet in force. They are subject to a public comment process until January 5, 2027, with public hearings scheduled for January 25. Forbes India reported that the US currently imposes an additional 10 percent tariff on many Indian goods, and that the proposed rate would be calculated net of certain existing Section 301 duties rather than simply added on top. For exporters in the flagged sectors — textiles, steel, solar modules and auto products among them — the comment window and the bilateral trade talks are the two tracks to watch.
